claim: The fly head cuticle has high transmission at wavelengths >900nm.
source: Our measurements showed that the fly head cuticle has surprisingly high transmission at wavelengths >900nm, and the difficulty of through-cuticle imaging is due to the air sacs and/or fat tissue underneath the head cuticle.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental measurements of optical transmission through the cuticle at various wavelengths.

claim: The difficulty of through-cuticle imaging is due to the air sacs and/or fat tissue underneath the head cuticle.
source: Our measurements showed that the fly head cuticle has surprisingly high transmission at wavelengths >900nm, and the difficulty of through-cuticle imaging is due to the air sacs and/or fat tissue underneath the head cuticle.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that removing or compressing air sacs improves imaging quality.

claim: 2-photon and 3-photon imaging are comparable in superficial regions such as the mushroom body.
source: Our anatomical and functional imaging results show that 2- and 3-photon imaging are comparable in superficial regions such as the mushroom body, but 3-photon imaging is superior in deeper regions such as the central complex and beyond.
evidence: This claim is supported by direct comparison of 2P and 3P imaging data in the mushroom body region.

claim: 3-photon imaging is superior in deeper regions such as the central complex and beyond.
source: Our anatomical and functional imaging results show that 2- and 3-photon imaging are comparable in superficial regions such as the mushroom body, but 3-photon imaging is superior in deeper regions such as the central complex and beyond.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data showing better signal-to-background ratio and resolution for 3P imaging at depth.

claim: Through-cuticle imaging method extends the time limits of in vivo imaging in flies.
source: The through-cuticle imaging method developed here extends the time limits of in vivo imaging in flies and opens new ways to capture neural structure and activity from the fly brain.
evidence: This claim is supported by demonstration of 12-hour continuous functional imaging experiments.

claim: Current methods used in fly optical physiology require the fly head cuticle, trachea, and fat body to be removed by microsurgery.
source: Current methods used in fly optical physiology require the fly head cuticle, trachea, and fat body to be removed by microsurgery to provide optical access to the nervous system (Grover et al., 2016; Minocci et al., 2013; Seelig et al., 2010; Sinha et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature describing standard imaging preparations.

claim: Current imaging preparations are limited in imaging duration because brain tissue starts to degenerate due to damaged circulation resulting from cuticle removal surgery.
source: These preparations are limited in imaging duration because, after some time, the brain tissue starts to degenerate due to damaged circulation resulting from the cuticle removal surgery.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the limitations of current methods and is supported by the cited example of olfactory neuron responses.

claim: Fly olfactory neurons show reliable Ca2+ responses for four to five hours after surgery with current imaging preparations.
source: For example, with current imaging preparations, fly olfactory neurons show reliable Ca2+ responses for four to five hours after surgery (Wang et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: 3-photon microscopy with long-wavelength lasers improves signal-to-background ratio by several orders of magnitude compared to 2-photon imaging methods.
source: A recent development in multiphoton imaging is the use of long-wavelength lasers in 3-photon (3P) microscopy which improves signal-to-background ratio (SBR) by several orders of magnitude compared to current 2-photon (2P) imaging methods (Horton et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2018a; Wang et al., 2018b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on 3P microscopy.

claim: 3-photon microscopy with 1700 nm excitation of red fluorophores and adaptive optics has shown promising results in imaging the fly brain through the cuticle.
source: While 3P microscopy with 1700 nm excitation of red fluorophores and adaptive optics has shown promising results in imaging the fly brain through the cuticle (Tao et al., 2017), it is not clear if the technique is widely applicable to common blue and green fluorophores with much shorter excitation wavelengths (e.g. 1320 nm).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Tao et al.

claim: It is not clear if 3P microscopy is widely applicable to common blue and green fluorophores with excitation wavelengths around 1320 nm.
source: While 3P microscopy with 1700 nm excitation of red fluorophores and adaptive optics has shown promising results in imaging the fly brain through the cuticle (Tao et al., 2017), it is not clear if the technique is widely applicable to common blue and green fluorophores with much shorter excitation wavelengths (e.g. 1320 nm).
evidence: This claim represents a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: The ballistic transmission through the fly head cuticle was high, reaching >90% at 1300 nm.
source: We found that for all the IR wavelengths tested, the ballistic transmission through the cuticle was high, reaching >90% at 1300 nm (Figure 1D, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Ballistic photon attenuation by the fly cuticle does not limit multiphoton imaging through the intact cuticle.
source: Since fluorescence signal within the focal volume in 2P and 3P microscopy is mostly generated by the ballistic photons (Dong et al., 2003; Horton et al., 2013), our results showed that ballistic photon attenuation by the fly cuticle does not limit multiphoton imaging through the intact cuticle.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data combined with cited knowledge about multiphoton microscopy.

claim: The total transmission through the head cuticle generally increased with wavelength.
source: Similar to the ballistic transmission experiments, we found that the total transmission generally increased with wavelength (Figure 1G, Figure 1—source data 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The total transmission for both green and red wavelengths was sufficiently high (>60%) for practical epi-fluorescence imaging using 2P or 3P excitation.
source: and the total transmission for both the green and red wavelengths was sufficiently high ( >60%) for practical epi-fluorescence imaging using 2P or 3P excitation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of total transmission.

claim: Absorption and scattering of long-wavelength light by the Drosophila head cuticle is small.
source: Our results demonstrated that absorption and scattering of long-wavelength light by the Drosophila head cuticle is small, and cuticle-intact in vivo imaging of green (e.g. green fluorescent protein (GFP) and GCaMP) and red fluorophores (e.g. red fluorescent protein (RFP), and RCaMP) through the intact cuticle is possible in adult flies using 2P or 3P excitation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the transmission measurements showing high transmission values.

claim: Cuticle-intact in vivo imaging of green and red fluorophores through the intact cuticle is possible in adult flies using 2P or 3P excitation.
source: Our results demonstrated that absorption and scattering of long-wavelength light by the Drosophila head cuticle is small, and cuticle-intact in vivo imaging of green (e.g. green fluorescent protein (GFP) and GCaMP) and red fluorophores (e.g. red fluorescent protein (RFP), and RCaMP) through the intact cuticle is possible in adult flies using 2P or 3P excitation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental demonstration of imaging through the cuticle.

claim: Head compression drastically improved image quality during through-cuticle imaging.
source: Compressing the head against the cover glass with forceps during the curing process drastically improved image quality (Figure 2E–G), mushroom body lobes were visible in the semi compressed and full compressed preparations in both 2P and 3P imaged flies.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of images with and without head compression shown in Figure 2.

claim: Flies behaved similarly with no head compression or in semi compressed preparations but not in full compression.
source: Based on our observations of the leg movements, flies behaved similarly with no head compression or in semi compressed preparations but not in full compression.
evidence: This claim is based on observational data of fly behavior.

claim: Semi head compression does not affect male courtship behavior grossly.
source: Our results showed that semi head compression does not affect male courtship behavior grossly; head-compressed males are able to copulate with females at similar rates as control males (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by courtship assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The tissue that interferes with 2P and 3P laser light is not the cuticle itself but the air sacs and other tissues that are between the head cuticle and the brain.
source: Our results demonstrated that the tissue that interferes with 2P and 3P laser light is not the cuticle itself but the air sacs and other tissues that are between the head cuticle and the brain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments showing improved imaging after air sac removal.

claim: The effective attenuation length for 2P excitation at 920 nm is 41.7 µm within depth 1-100 µm.
source: We further quantified the effective attenuation length (EAL) for 2P and 3P excitation, and we found EAL920nm = 41.7 µm, EAL1320nm = 59.4 µm within depth 1–100 µm, and EAL1320nm = 91.7 µm within depth 100–180 µm (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The effective attenuation length for 3P excitation at 1320 nm is 59.4 µm within depth 1-100 µm.
source: We further quantified the effective attenuation length (EAL) for 2P and 3P excitation, and we found EAL920nm = 41.7 µm, EAL1320nm = 59.4 µm within depth 1–100 µm, and EAL1320nm = 91.7 µm within depth 100–180 µm (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The effective attenuation length for 3P excitation at 1320 nm is 91.7 µm within depth 100-180 µm.
source: We further quantified the effective attenuation length (EAL) for 2P and 3P excitation, and we found EAL920nm = 41.7 µm, EAL1320nm = 59.4 µm within depth 1–100 µm, and EAL1320nm = 91.7 µm within depth 100–180 µm (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The FWHM of the lateral brightness distribution at 200 µm below the surface of the cuticle was ~1.4 µm for tracheal branches captured by the THG signal.
source: The full width at half maximum (FWHM) of the lateral brightness distribution at 200 µm below the surface of the cuticle was ~1.4 µm for tracheal branches captured by the THG signal (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by resolution measurements shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Similarity in the attenuation lengths of THG and 3P fluorescence signal indicates that the labeling of membrane-targeted GFP is uniform across the brain.
source: Similarity in the attenuation lengths of THG and 3P fluorescence signal indicates that the labeling of membrane-targeted GFP is uniform across the brain, validating the use of the fluorescence signal when quantifying the EALs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the comparison of THG and fluorescence attenuation.

claim: Removing the cuticle and underlying tissues increased the EAL by ~1.5×.
source: We measured the EAL for both cuticle-removed and cuticle-intact 2P/3P imaging and found that removing the cuticle and underlying tissues increased the EAL by ~1.5× (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The cuticle-removed imaging preparation generated images with ~1.5× better axial resolution compared to cuticle-intact imaging preparations for both 2P and 3P imaging.
source: Our measurements showed that the cuticle-removed imaging preparation generated images with ~1.5× better axial resolution compared to cuticle-intact imaging preparations for both 2P and 3-P imaging (Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 2—source data 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by resolution measurements shown in supplementary figures.

claim: 3P imaging showed the same axial resolution in the mushroom body (~50 µm) and central complex (~100 µm).
source: 3P imaging showed the same axial resolution in the mushroom body (~50 µm) and central complex (~100 µm) while 2P imaging showed a deterioration of axial resolution for deep imaging in the central complex (Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by resolution measurements at different depths.

claim: 2P imaging showed a deterioration of axial resolution for deep imaging in the central complex.
source: 3P imaging showed the same axial resolution in the mushroom body (~50 µm) and central complex (~100 µm) while 2P imaging showed a deterioration of axial resolution for deep imaging in the central complex (Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by resolution measurements at different depths.

claim: The average motion measured during through-cuticle imaging was 1.3 µm, which is much smaller than the size of a fly neuron (~5 µm).
source: The average motion measured was 1.3 µm, which is much smaller than the size of a fly neuron (~5 µm) (Figure 3—figure supplement 4. Figure 3—figure supplement 4—source data 1Figure 3—figure supplement 4—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by motion tracking measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Motion is not an issue during through-cuticle imaging at depths investigated.
source: Based on our results, we concluded that motion is not an issue during through-cuticle imaging at depths we have investigated.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the motion measurements.

claim: Both 2P and 3P excitation can be used for through-cuticle imaging at the superficial layers of the fly brain such as the mushroom body.
source: Together our results demonstrate that although both 2P and 3P excitation can be used for through-cuticle imaging at the superficial layers of the fly brain such as the mushroom body, 3P outperforms 2P in deeper brain regions such as the central complex especially when cellular and subcellular resolutions are necessary.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative imaging data at different depths.

claim: 3P outperforms 2P in deeper brain regions such as the central complex especially when cellular and subcellular resolutions are necessary.
source: Together our results demonstrate that although both 2P and 3P excitation can be used for through-cuticle imaging at the superficial layers of the fly brain such as the mushroom body, 3P outperforms 2P in deeper brain regions such as the central complex especially when cellular and subcellular resolutions are necessary.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative imaging data showing better resolution and contrast for 3P at depth.

claim: This conclusion is consistent with imaging studies conducted in the mouse brain.
source: This conclusion is consistent with the imaging studies conducted in the mouse brain (Mok et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2018a; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work in mouse brain imaging.

claim: There was no measurable heat-stress response detected by HSP70 protein levels when flies were exposed to 2P (920 nm) and 3P (1320 nm) excitation at 15 mW for 24 min.
source: Our results showed that there was no measurable heat-stress response detected by the HSP70 protein levels when flies were exposed to 2P (920 nm) and 3P (1320 nm) excitation at 15 mW for 24 min (four 6-min intervals, see methods for details) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Increasing laser power to 25 mW for 3P caused a significant increase in HSP70 protein levels in the fly brain.
source: However, increasing laser power to 25 mW for 3P caused a significant increase in HSP70 protein levels in the fly brain (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: 2P and 3P cuticle-intact imaging is safe at power levels below 15 mW.
source: These results suggest that 2P and 3P cuticle-intact imaging is safe at power levels below 15 mW, similar to power levels used for 2P cuticle-removed imaging.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the HSP70 expression data.

claim: The depth limit for 3P cuticle-intact imaging was ~120 µm.
source: 3P cuticle-removed preparation allowed us to image down to ~250 µm deep (Figure 4B), while the depth limit for 3P cuticle-intact imaging was ~120 µm (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claim: 3P cuticle-removed preparation allowed imaging down to ~250 µm deep.
source: 3P cuticle-removed preparation allowed us to image down to ~250 µm deep (Figure 4B), while the depth limit for 3P cuticle-intact imaging was ~120 µm (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The depth limit for 2P functional imaging through the cuticle was ~65 µm.
source: The depth limit for 2P functional imaging through the cuticle was ~65 µm, while cuticle-removed imaging allowed optical access to ~120 µm (Figure 4C and D, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Cuticle-removed 2P imaging allowed optical access to ~120 µm.
source: The depth limit for 2P functional imaging through the cuticle was ~65 µm, while cuticle-removed imaging allowed optical access to ~120 µm (Figure 4C and D, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The presence of the cuticle and the underlying tissue decreases 2P and 3P functional imaging depth in the brain by ~2× and reduces dF/F0.
source: These results suggested that the presence of the cuticle and the underlying tissue decreases 2P and 3P functional imaging depth in the brain by ~2× and reduces dF/Fo.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of imaging depths between cuticle-intact and cuticle-removed preparations.

claim: No significant differences were observed in neural activity in responses to food odor stimulation across different compartments of the γ-lobes or between 2P and 3P excitation of GCaMP6s.
source: No significant differences were observed in neural activity in responses to food odor stimulation across different compartments of the γ-lobes or between 2P and 3P excitation of GCaMP6s (Figure 5G-I, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional imaging data comparing 2P and 3P responses shown in Figure 5.

claim: Both 2P and 3P excitation can be used to image odor responses from mushroom body γ-lobes using through-cuticle imaging.
source: Our data demonstrated that both 2P and 3P excitation can be used to image odor responses from mushroom body γ-lobes using through-cuticle imaging but for cell body imaging 3P excitation is preferred.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional imaging data showing odor responses with both methods.

claim: For cell body imaging, 3P excitation is preferred.
source: Our data demonstrated that both 2P and 3P excitation can be used to image odor responses from mushroom body γ-lobes using through-cuticle imaging but for cell body imaging 3P excitation is preferred.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data showing better cell body resolution with 3P.

claim: After brief exposure to food odor stimulus, flies increased their forward walking speed and turning rate.
source: We further analyzed the odor-evoked changes in fly walking behavior and showed that after the brief exposure to food odor stimulus, flies increased their forward walking speed and turning rate (Figure 6E–G, Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Odor-evoked behavioral responses lasted for multiple seconds.
source: These responses lasted for multiple seconds (Figure 6H–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 6.

claim: There is a significant difference between the average forward and rotational speed values before and after the food odor exposure.
source: Moreover, statistical analysis showed that there is a significant difference between the average forward and rotational speed values before and after the food odor exposure (Figure 6I and K, Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Head-compressed flies in the spherical treadmill setup can walk and exhibit behavioral and neural responses to odor stimulation.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that head-compressed flies in our spherical treadmill setup can walk and exhibit behavioral and neural responses to odor stimulation.
evidence: This claim is based on the combined behavioral and imaging data from the treadmill experiments.

claim: The odor-evoked neural responses did not change with food and water deprivation in any of the γ-lobe compartments imaged during 12-hour chronic imaging.
source: Our analysis showed that the odor-evoked neural responses did not change with food and water deprivation in any of the γ-lobe compartments imaged (Figure 7, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by chronic functional imaging data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The cuticle-intact imaging method allows recording of neural activity within an individual fly over long time scales (12 hr).
source: These results suggest that the cuticle-intact imaging method developed here allows recording of neural activity within an individual fly over long time scales (12 hr), which was previously not possible with commonly used cuticle-removed imaging preparations.
evidence: This claim is supported by demonstration of 12-hour continuous functional imaging.

claim: Imaging through the fly cuticle was considered to be not feasible at wavelengths typically used for 2P (~920 nm) and 3P (~1300 nm) imaging because of concerns about cuticle absorption.
source: Imaging through the fly cuticle was considered to be not feasible at the wavelengths typically used for 2P ( ~ 920 nm) and 3P ( ~ 1300 nm) imaging because of concerns about cuticle absorption (Lin et al., 2015; Tao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature expressing this concern.

claim: It is not the absorption by the cuticle but rather the opacity of the air sacs and the tissues located between the head cuticle and the brain that limit the penetration depth of multiphoton imaging.
source: We found that it is not the absorption by the cuticle but rather the opacity of the air sacs and the tissues located between the head cuticle and the brain that limit the penetration depth of multiphoton imaging (Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments showing improved imaging after air sac manipulation.

claim: Semi head compression does not cause measurable differences in fly courtship or olfactory behaviors.
source: Careful assessments showed that semi head compression does not cause measurable differences in fly courtship (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), or olfactory behaviors (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral assay data.

claim: Long excitation wavelength (e.g. ~1700 nm) is not necessary for imaging the fly brain through the cuticle.
source: Our results clearly demonstrate that long excitation wavelength (e.g. ~1700 nm) is not necessary for imaging the fly brain through the cuticle and our fly preparations enable cuticle-intact 2P and 3P imaging of common fluorophores (e.g. GFP and GCaMPs) at 920 nm and 1320 nm, respectively (Figures 2—7).
evidence: This claim is supported by successful imaging at shorter wavelengths demonstrated throughout the results.

claim: The through-cuticle imaging method significantly extends the time frame of current in vivo imaging preparations used for anatomical and functional studies in fly neuroscience.
source: The through-cuticle imaging method developed here significantly extends the time frame of current in vivo imaging preparations used for anatomical and functional studies in fly neuroscience.
evidence: This claim is supported by demonstration of 12-hour continuous imaging compared to 4-5 hour limits of current methods.

claim: The imaging method will allow researchers to capture the activity of neural populations during changing behavioral states.
source: Our imaging method will allow researchers to capture the activity of neural populations during changing behavioral states; facilitate decoding of neural plasticity during memory formation; and might permit observation of changes in brain structures during development and aging.
evidence: This claim is speculative about future applications of the method.

claim: The imaging method will facilitate decoding of neural plasticity during memory formation.
source: Our imaging method will allow researchers to capture the activity of neural populations during changing behavioral states; facilitate decoding of neural plasticity during memory formation; and might permit observation of changes in brain structures during development and aging.
evidence: This claim is speculative about future applications of the method.

claim: The imaging method might permit observation of changes in brain structures during development and aging.
source: Our imaging method will allow researchers to capture the activity of neural populations during changing behavioral states; facilitate decoding of neural plasticity during memory formation; and might permit observation of changes in brain structures during development and aging.
evidence: This claim is speculative about future applications of the method.

claim: Odor-evoked Ca2+ responses did not change during repeated odor stimulation over 12 hours.
source: Our results suggest that odor-evoked Ca2+ responses did not change during the repeated odor stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by chronic functional imaging data showing stable responses over time.

claim: Even longer imaging time than 12 hours is possible by feeding flies under the microscope.
source: Even longer imaging time is possible by feeding flies under the microscope.
evidence: This claim is speculative about extending the imaging duration.

claim: Conventional 2P microscopy has adequate penetration depth for imaging the behavioral responses within the mushroom body.
source: We performed 2P imaging for demonstrating the possibility of long-term recording of neural activity because conventional 2P microscopy has adequate penetration depth for imaging the behavioral responses within the mushroom body, and 2P microscopy is widely used by the fly neuroscience community.
evidence: This claim is based on the imaging data showing successful 2P imaging of the mushroom body.

claim: 2P microscopy is widely used by the fly neuroscience community.
source: We performed 2P imaging for demonstrating the possibility of long-term recording of neural activity because conventional 2P microscopy has adequate penetration depth for imaging the behavioral responses within the mushroom body, and 2P microscopy is widely used by the fly neuroscience community.
evidence: This claim is based on general knowledge of the field.

claim: Combination of cuticle-intact fly preparation and 3P imaging may provide the possibility of long-term imaging in deeper regions of the fly brain such as the central complex.
source: On the other hand, our deep functional imaging data (Figure 4) showed that combination of our cuticle-intact fly preparation and 3P imaging may provide the exciting possibility of long-term imaging in deeper regions of the fly brain such as the central complex.
evidence: This claim is speculative about future applications based on the deep imaging results.

claim: The success rate of chronic imaging experiments was ~50% because of drift in the axial position of the brain when imaging for long periods of time.
source: We note that the success rate of chronic imaging experiments was ~50% because of the drift in the axial position of the brain when imaging for long periods of time.
evidence: This claim is based on empirical observation during chronic imaging experiments.

claim: Further optimizations might improve the success rate of chronic imaging.
source: Further optimizations might improve the success rate of chronic imaging.
evidence: This claim is speculative about future improvements.

claim: There will be a wide variety of uses for this technology in Drosophila neuroscience research.
source: We anticipate that there will be a wide variety of uses for this technology in Drosophila neuroscience research.
evidence: This claim is speculative about future applications of the method.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster offers an ideal experimental system to investigate neural correlates of behavioral states and decisions because of its compact nervous system and diverse state-dependent behaviors.
source: The fly, Drosophila melanogaster, offers an ideal experimental system to investigate neural correlates of behavioral states and decisions because of its compact nervous system and diverse state-dependent behaviors that it executes in response to sensory stimuli (Barron et al., 2015; Dickson, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: It is critical to capture the activity of populations of neurons over long time scales as flies are changing their physiological needs to understand how molecularly defined neural circuits evaluate sensory information in different behavioral states.
source: To understand how molecularly defined neural circuits evaluate sensory information in different behavioral states, it is critical to capture the activity of populations of neurons over long time scales as flies are changing their physiological needs (Luo et al., 2018; Simpson and Looger, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and represents a motivation for the study.

claim: Functional imaging experiments require imaging preparations which should allow chronic neural activity imaging for at least 12 hr.
source: These functional imaging experiments require imaging preparations, which should allow chronic neural activity imaging for at least 12 hr.
evidence: This claim represents a requirement that motivates the development of the new method.

claim: In mice, multiday imaging experiments are achieved by implanting a cranial window following removal of part of the skull.
source: In mice, multiday imaging experiments are achieved by implanting a cranial window following removal of part of the skull (Hefendehl et al., 2012; Trachtenberg et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work in mouse imaging.

claim: Similar imaging preparations have been developed for flies.
source: Similar imaging preparations have been developed for flies (Grover et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2018; Sinha et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Imaging window implantation requires a tedious surgery with low success rates and complications that occur afterwards.
source: However, because imaging window implantation requires a tedious surgery with low success rates and complications that occur afterwards, these methods are not commonly used.
evidence: This claim is based on general knowledge of the limitations of window implantation methods.

claim: Window implantation methods are not commonly used in fly imaging.
source: However, because imaging window implantation requires a tedious surgery with low success rates and complications that occur afterwards, these methods are not commonly used.
evidence: This claim is based on general knowledge of the field.

claim: Kenyon cells are the primary intrinsic neurons in the insect mushroom body.
source: Kenyon cells are the primary intrinsic neurons in the insect mushroom body.
evidence: This claim represents established anatomical knowledge.

claim: There are approximately 2200 Kenyon cells in Drosophila.
source: Diverse subtypes of Kenyon cells (n = ~2200) extend their axons along the pedunculus and in the dorsal and medial lobes (Crittenden et al., 1998; Ito et al., 1998; Strausfeld et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: Kenyon cells receive and integrate information from heterogeneous sets of projection neurons which carry olfactory, gustatory, and visual sensory information.
source: These neurons receive and integrate information from heterogeneous sets of projection neurons which carry olfactory, gustatory, and visual sensory information (Owald and Waddell, 2015; Yagi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on mushroom body connectivity.

claim: Kenyon cell dendrites arborize in the calyx.
source: Kenyon cell dendrites arborize in the calyx, while their axons fasciculate into anatomically distinct structures called lobes, with the dorsal lobes forming α and α′ branches, and the medial lobes containing β, β′, and γ branches (Crittenden et al., 1998; Ito et al., 1998; Zheng et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: Kenyon cell axons fasciculate into anatomically distinct structures called lobes, with the dorsal lobes forming α and α′ branches, and the medial lobes containing β, β′, and γ branches.
source: Kenyon cell dendrites arborize in the calyx, while their axons fasciculate into anatomically distinct structures called lobes, with the dorsal lobes forming α and α′ branches, and the medial lobes containing β, β′, and γ branches (Crittenden et al., 1998; Ito et al., 1998; Zheng et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: The insect central complex is a brain neuropil which processes sensory information and guides a diverse set of behavioral responses.
source: The insect central complex is a brain neuropil which processes sensory information and guides a diverse set of behavioral responses (Pfeiffer and Homberg, 2014; Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015; Wolff et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on central complex function.

claim: The central complex is composed of anatomically distinct compartments: the protocerebral bridge, ellipsoid body, fan-shaped body, and the noduli.
source: It is composed of anatomically distinct compartments: the protocerebral bridge, ellipsoid body, fan-shaped body, and the noduli (Wolff et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous anatomical work.

claim: The ellipsoid body consists of a group of neurons, the ring neurons, that extend their axons to the midline forming a ring-like structure.
source: The ellipsoid body consists of a group of neurons, the ring neurons, that extend their axons to the midline forming a ring-like structure (Pfeiffer and Homberg, 2014; Wolff et al., 2015; Xie et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: The FWHM of the lateral brightness distribution measured by a ring neuron's neurite cross-section was ~1.2 µm for the fluorescent signal.
source: The FWHM of the lateral brightness distribution measured by a ring neuron's neurite cross-section was ~1.2 µm for the fluorescent signal (Figure 3F)
evidence: This claim is supported by resolution measurements shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The FWHM of the lateral brightness distribution was ~0.8 µm for tracheal branches captured by the THG signal.
source: and ~0.8 µm for tracheal branches captured by the THG signal (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by resolution measurements shown in Figure 3G.

claim: During food odor exposure, hungry flies increase their walking speed, orient, and walk toward the odor stimulus.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that during food odor exposure, hungry flies increase their walking speed, orient, and walk toward the odor stimulus.
evidence: This claim is based on previous studies of fly behavior.

claim: After odor stimulation, flies increase their turning rate which resembles local search behavior.
source: After odor stimulation, however, flies increase their turning rate which resembles local search behavior.
evidence: This claim is based on previous studies of fly behavior.

claim: The odor offset responses persist for multiple seconds after the odor exposure.
source: The odor offset responses persist for multiple seconds after the odor exposure (Álvarez-Salvado et al., 2018; Sayin et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous behavioral studies.

claim: Semi head-compressed flies increase their turning rate upon brief stimulation with food odor apple cider vinegar.
source: In our experiments with semi head-compressed flies, flies increase their turning rate upon brief stimulation with food odor apple cider vinegar (Figure 6B, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Odor-evoked neural responses from all mushroom body γ-lobe compartments were reliably captured during behavioral experiments.
source: During these experiments, we were able to capture odor-evoked neural responses from all mushroom body γ-lobe compartments reliably (Figure 6C, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The results are in agreement with previous studies that quantified odor-induced changes in walking behavior in head-fixed flies.
source: Our results are in agreement with previous studies that quantified odor-induced changes in walking behavior in head-fixed flies (Sayin et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to cited previous work.

claim: Within the wavelength range of 350–1000 nm, the relative transmission of the dorsal head cuticle of D. melanogaster improves with increasing wavelengths.
source: Previous experiments showed that, within the wavelength range of 350–1000 nm, the relative transmission of the dorsal head cuticle of D. melanogaster improves with increasing wavelengths (Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The absolute transmission through the cuticle, which is critical for assessing the practicality of through-cuticle imaging, was not reported in previous studies.
source: However, the absolute transmission, which is critical for assessing the practicality of through-cuticle imaging, was not reported.
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in previous literature that the current study addresses.

claim: Fluorescence signal within the focal volume in 2P and 3P microscopy is mostly generated by the ballistic photons.
source: Since fluorescence signal within the focal volume in 2P and 3P microscopy is mostly generated by the ballistic photons (Dong et al., 2003; Horton et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on multiphoton microscopy.

claim: Based on dopaminergic innervation, γ-lobes can be subdivided into five anatomical compartments.
source: Based on dopaminergic innervation, γ-lobes can be subdivided into five anatomical compartments (Cohn et al., 2015; Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous anatomical work and illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: Placing flies in a 30°C incubator for 10 minutes caused a significant increase in HSP70 protein levels across the fly brain.
source: In contrast, placing flies in a 30°C incubator for 10 minutes caused a significant increase in HSP70 protein levels across the fly brain (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Flies that were kept at room temperature had low levels of the HSP70 protein.
source: Flies that were kept at room temperature had low levels of the HSP70 protein (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The recommended power level for 2P imaging of fly neural activity with cuticle-removed preparations is ~15 mW.
source: The recommended power level for 2P imaging of fly neural activity with cuticle-removed preparations is ~15 mW (Seelig et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: 3P excitation can induce heating in the mouse brain at high laser powers.
source: 3P excitation can induce heating in the mouse brain at high laser powers (Wang et al., 2018a; Wang et al., 2018b; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on 3P imaging in mice.

claim: HSP70 protein levels reflect heat-induced stress in the fly brain.
source: We first tested whether HSP70 protein levels reflect heat-induced stress in the fly brain.
evidence: This claim is tested and confirmed by the heat shock experiments showing HSP70 elevation at 30°C.

claim: For cuticle-removed fly, 3P requires 1.4 nJ and 2P requires 0.2 nJ on the brain surface to image the mushroom body.
source: For cuticle-removed fly, 3P requires 1.4 nJ and 2P requires 0.2 nJ on the brain surface to image the mushroom body.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative power measurements.

claim: For cuticle-intact fly, 3P requires 3.0 nJ and 2P requires 0.5 nJ on the cuticle surface to image the mushroom body.
source: For cuticle-intact fly, 3P requires 3.0 nJ and 2P requires 0.5 nJ on the cuticle surface to image the mushroom body.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative power measurements.

claim: In the superficial layers of the fly brain (~50 µm), through-cuticle 2P and 3P imaging generated images with similar signal-to-background ratio to cuticle-removed preparation.
source: We found that in the superficial layers of the fly brain (i.e. ~50 µm), through-cuticle 2P and 3P imaging generated images with similar signal-to-background ratio (SBR) to cuticle-removed preparation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 3P generated images with better SBR compared to 2P in both cuticle-intact and cuticle-removed preparations.
source: 3P generated images with better SBR compared to 2P in both cuticle-intact and cuticle-removed preparations.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative imaging data.

claim: Within ~100 μm depth, 2P imaging provided reasonable contrast when imaging through intact cuticle.
source: Within ~100 μm depth, 2P imaging provided reasonable contrast when imaging through intact cuticle.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data at various depths.

claim: 3P imaging shows an increase in background that degrades image contrast when imaging beyond the esophagus (~150 μm).
source: While imaging is still possible with 3P at the subesophageal zone ( >150 μm), it shows an increase in background that degrades image contrast when imaging beyond the esophagus (~150 μm).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data at depth showing degraded contrast.

claim: When cuticle was removed, 2P imaging depth increased to ~180 μm.
source: When cuticle was removed, 2P imaging depth increased to ~180 μm, and 3P imaging depth increased to ~300 μm, reaching to the bottom of the fly brain.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data from cuticle-removed preparations.

claim: When cuticle was removed, 3P imaging depth increased to ~300 μm, reaching to the bottom of the fly brain.
source: When cuticle was removed, 2P imaging depth increased to ~180 μm, and 3P imaging depth increased to ~300 μm, reaching to the bottom of the fly brain.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data from cuticle-removed preparations.

claim: The average odor stimulus latency to peak odor amplitude was <100 ms across 34 measurements.
source: We sampled odor delivery using the PID every 20 ms and found average latency to peak odor amplitude was <100 ms across 34 measurements.
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements using a photo ionization detector.
